news_summary: Ancient cave art has been discovered, revealing hidden prehistoric creativity preserved for 26,000 years.
news_summary_fr: Des peintures rupestres anciennes ont été découvertes, révélant une créativité préhistorique insoupçonnée, préservée depuis 26 000 ans.
news_summary_es: Se ha descubierto arte rupestre antiguo que revela una creatividad prehistórica oculta y conservada durante 26 000 años.

articles.title: The palaeo cave art that hid in plain sight for 26,000 years
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03585-zHundreds of engravings were spotted in a widely visited cave — some include signs of animation.
articles.content:
Inscriptions at the Cova de la Font Major cave system in Catalonia in northeastern Spain prompts rethink of prehistoric population and cultural trends. Credit: Vergès Bosch, J. M., Salas-Altès, M./Antiquity

Archaeologists have described hundreds of rock-art engravings dating back around 26,000 years in a cave frequently visited by tourists in Catalonia — a region of northeastern Spain that was thought to be almost devoid of palaeolithic art1. The findings were published in the journal Antiquity on 5 November.

Josep Maria Vergès Bosch, an archaeologist at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES-CERCA) in Tarragona, Spain, spotted some prehistoric engravings among more-modern graffiti in the Cova de la Font Major during a planned excavation in 2019.

Vergès and archaeologist Míriam Salas-Altès at IPHES-CERCA studied 280 Palaeolithic art motifs, including 55 animal depictions, from the cave. “The sheer quantity of art discovered at the Cova de la Font Major is exceptional,” says Salas-Altès.

Early animation

The cave system — made up of more than 3.5 kilometres of underground passageways that have been occupied numerous times during human history — has been open to the public for some seven decades and became a museum in the 1990s.

The drawings were easy to miss. “When you shine a light straight on the engravings, they are really difficult to see, you have to play with light from different directions to see the depressions,” says Salas-Altès.

Researcher Míriam Salas-Altès documents engravings in a tunnel of the cave system. Credit: Josep Maria Vergès/IPHES-CERCA

The etchings include images of animals such as a horse, a bear and an aurochs (the ancestor of domestic cattle), as well as myriad swirling lines. A handful of the engravings reveal how the artists used “natural lines or fissures in the walls”, says Salas-Altès. For example, “one is used to represent the ground under a horse”.
articles.reasoning: The discovery of hundreds of previously unnoticed 26,000-year-old palaeo cave engravings in a well-visited cave in Catalonia provides significant new insights into prehistoric human culture and art. This finding has broad cultural and historical significance, enriching our understanding of early human creativity and population trends. The article focuses on a single, well-documented archaeological discovery with meaningful impact for the general public's knowledge of human history.
articles.personality_title: Hundreds of 26,000-year-old cave engravings found in busy Catalonia cave
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Cova de la Font Major cave in Catalonia, Spain, has been a popular tourist spot and museum for decades. Until recently, experts believed this area had very little prehistoric cave art.

**What happened** – In 2019, archaeologists Josep Maria Vergès Bosch and Míriam Salas-Altès discovered hundreds of ancient engravings inside the cave. These markings, some showing animals like horses and bears, are about 26,000 years old. The art was hard to see because it blends with modern graffiti and is only visible when light shines at certain angles.

**Impact** – This discovery changes what scientists thought about prehistoric humans in this region. Finding so many detailed engravings in a well-known cave shows that early humans here were more creative and active than previously believed. It also gives new clues about their culture and how they used natural features of the cave walls in their art.

**What's next step** – Researchers will continue studying the engravings to learn more about their meaning and how they were made. The cave might also be studied further to find other hidden artworks, helping us better understand life during the Paleolithic era.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Hundreds of ancient engravings hidden in a popular Catalan cave reveal surprising new details about prehistoric human art and culture.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des centaines de gravures vieilles de 26 000 ans découvertes dans une grotte très fréquentée de Catalogne
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La grotte Cova de la Font Major en Catalogne, Espagne, est un lieu touristique et un musée connu depuis des décennies. Jusqu’à récemment, on pensait que cette région avait très peu d’art préhistorique.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En 2019, les archéologues Josep Maria Vergès Bosch et Míriam Salas-Altès ont découvert des centaines de gravures anciennes dans la grotte. Ces dessins, représentant des animaux comme des chevaux et des ours, datent d’environ 26 000 ans. L’art était difficile à voir car il se confond avec des graffitis modernes et n’est visible qu’avec une lumière venant sous certains angles.

**Impact** – Cette découverte change la vision des scientifiques sur les hommes préhistoriques dans cette région. Trouver autant de gravures détaillées dans une grotte bien connue montre que ces premiers humains étaient plus créatifs et actifs que ce que l’on croyait. Cela apporte aussi de nouvelles informations sur leur culture et leur manière d’utiliser les formes naturelles des murs pour leur art.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont continuer à étudier les gravures pour mieux comprendre leur sens et leur création. La grotte pourrait aussi être explorée davantage pour trouver d’autres œuvres cachées, ce qui aidera à mieux connaître la vie à l’époque paléolithique.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des centaines de gravures anciennes cachées dans une grotte catalane populaire révèlent de nouveaux détails surprenants sur l’art et la culture des hommes préhistoriques.
articles.personality_title_es: Cientos de grabados de 26 000 años hallados en una cueva muy visitada de Cataluña
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La cueva Cova de la Font Major en Cataluña, España, ha sido un lugar turístico y museo durante décadas. Hasta hace poco, se pensaba que esta zona tenía muy poco arte prehistórico.

**Qué pasó** – En 2019, los arqueólogos Josep Maria Vergès Bosch y Míriam Salas-Altès descubrieron cientos de grabados antiguos en la cueva. Estas imágenes, que muestran animales como caballos y osos, tienen unos 26 000 años. El arte era difícil de ver porque se mezcla con grafitis modernos y solo se nota cuando la luz incide desde ciertos ángulos.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo cambia lo que los científicos pensaban sobre los humanos prehistóricos en esta región. Encontrar tantos grabados detallados en una cueva conocida muestra que los primeros humanos aquí eran más creativos y activos de lo que se creía. También da nuevas pistas sobre su cultura y cómo usaban las formas naturales de las paredes en su arte.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores seguirán estudiando los grabados para entender mejor su significado y cómo se hicieron. Es posible que se exploren más partes de la cueva para encontrar otras obras ocultas, ayudando a conocer mejor la vida en la era paleolítica.

**Resumen en una frase** – Cientos de grabados antiguos escondidos en una cueva catalana popular revelan nuevos detalles sorprendentes sobre el arte y la cultura de los humanos prehistóricos.
